doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Austin ballroom applause and a dangerous Florida hall
summary: Hungry stop on a broken-down bus, a standing ovation in Austin, and a West Palm Beach hall with the stand raised high.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: waiting and now it’s like 5 or 6:00 and the guys were getting hungry. So the manager was the white guy, Frenchie — excuse me, the ginger ale, it’s human, it’s real — so we said you know we just passed a diner about a hundred feet back there. So the guy that sold the programs, Frenchie and myself, we went there to get some food. We sat at the counter, we ate, and then we took out five or six, I don’t know, for the rest of the guys. I took orders, like when you work in an office in New York, whoever wants coffee, who has a cheeseburger. So we took out some blue plate specials. And we walked back to the bus and the guys ate in the bus see? Now the other bus comes, picks us up there, change buses, we get in the other bus and we get to this ballroom, so the bus pulls up in front of the ballroom, so we go in the front entrance, and the bandstand is way at the other end of the dance floor. So we walked in and walked and naturally there was like no music or anything so everybody’s sitting down at the tables. The dance floor is empty. We walked right across the dance floor, and the whole room got up, standing applause, because Louis is walking. And I said, “I can’t believe this. It’s weird. I can’t believe this is happening here.” You know these are the things that the first time I ever witnessed something like that in my lifetime. Because like I say prior to that I had always been with white bands and I never experienced anything like that. And well the funny thing happened once, we were in Florida and we were living in Miami and we had to do a one-nighter in West Palm Beach or something like that, not too far away. So I had a friend of mine who had a band down there and I had dinner with he and his wife and some friends of theirs. So his wife says, to me, “you know you’re doing a concert tomorrow night at West Palm Beach, can we come with you?” And I said, “gee I don’t know I’ll have to ask my manager, you know I don’t know what kind of situation it is.” So I called Frenchie. I said, “Frenchie, I’ve got some friends they would like to come to the concert.” He says, “how many people?” I said, “how many of you want to go?” So it was just his wife and her girlfriend said, we’d like to go with you. Okay, in fact she said, “we’ll drive you down there because we know exactly where the place is.” It was called something palace, but you should have seen the place, it was unbelievable. It was weird man. So anyway they drove me down there, and when we got in the place it was like a funky, like a social club, you know, where they have dances with the teenage stuff. It was a run down, broken down kind of place, and I looked for the bandstand and it was across the room and it was about

nine feet in the air. Like there was a balcony, a bandstand about eight or nine feet up, with a railing. I don’t even know if it had a railing, with an upright piano that was on a slant. Because the floor slanted this way toward the thing. So I went up on the bandstand and Bob says to me, “you’d better get those two girls and bring them up here, because it could get rough.” It could get rough. I says okay. They were both blondes too. I said, “hey girls, up here” so they come up and they sat on the bandstand all night with us.
Well you’ve got an education then.
Yeah, that was it you know. That’s when I learned what was happening.
